title: Elizabethan Witchcraft Act: Harm Required, Death Only for Murder
description: The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed in the fifth year of Elizabeth I's reign, restored witchcraft as a capital crime after the 1547 repeal while imposing significant evidentiary requirements. Unlike later legislation, the 1563 act required proof of actual harm: the death penalty was reserved for cases where witchcraft caused human death, while lesser offenses (injury, property damage, treasure-finding, provoking love) carried imprisonment for first offenses and death only on repetition. This requirement that harm be demonstrated — rather than diabolical conspiracy proved — produced a distinctly different pattern of prosecution from German procedure, focusing English trials on neighborhood disputes and actual complaints of maleficium rather than sweeping conspiracy prosecutions. The moderate 1563 standard helps explain the relatively low English execution rate compared to German territories.
historiographical_note: Alan Macfarlane's Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England (1970) and Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) both emphasized the 1563 act's focus on maleficium (demonstrated harm) as key to understanding the social pattern of English witch accusations — rooted in neighbor disputes over charity refusal. James Sharpe's subsequent work refined this model while preserving its central insight.
source_method: 5 Elizabeth I c.16 (1563); Macfarlane (1970); Thomas (1971); secondary scholarship on English witchcraft
